text: Four supply shapes dominate token design. Fixed supply sets a hard cap at genesis, with no mechanism ever minting more. Capped or disinflationary supply has a maximum, but mints toward it gradually, approaching asymptotically rather than all at once.

Inflationary, uncapped supply mints continuously with no ceiling, typically to fund staking rewards indefinitely. Deflationary supply actively shrinks over time through a burn mechanism, often funded by a cut of transaction fees. These aren't mutually exclusive — a capped token can still have a burn that makes its net inflation negative.

Max, total, and circulating supply are not the same number. Max supply is the hard ceiling. Total supply is everything minted so far, including locked or treasury-held tokens. Circulating supply is total supply minus anything locked, vesting, or held in treasury — the part that's actually freely tradeable right now.

Take a token with a billion-token max supply, 600 million minted so far, and 250 million of that locked in vesting or treasury. Circulating supply is only 350 million. Market cap figures that use total supply instead of circulating supply overstate how much is actually liquid.

A burn mechanism permanently destroys tokens, usually by sending them to an address nobody controls. Net supply change is emissions minted minus tokens burned. Mint 20 million in staking rewards, burn 25 million from transaction fees in the same year, and circulating supply actually shrinks by 5 million — even while the protocol keeps minting rewards.

That's the mechanism behind ultrasound-money designs: an inflationary reward schedule combined with a fee-driven burn large enough to make the net effect deflationary during high-activity periods. Next: utility versus governance tokens, and what determines which kind a protocol actually needs.
